tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Sir, all 4 articles opened and read in full via Firecrawl scrape (main content, markdown). Nothing failed. Page boilerplate (ads, comments) ignored. Note: these are short blog posts, so "full" is still modest.

**1. "What is BATNA? How to Find Your Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement"** (PON, adapted from G. Subramanian). Full text, ~480 words.
- BATNA is what you do if no deal happens. It decides whether to accept, how much leverage you have, and when to walk away.
- Negotiators fixate on the offer in front of them and forget their alternatives.
- Before comparing, translate both options into truly comparable terms. A headline price can hide worse coverage, exclusions or definitions.
- Example: an insurance quote 30% cheaper turned out worse once fine print was compared. The apparent BATNA was weaker than it looked.
- A BATNA is only as strong as your understanding of it. Misjudging it makes you reject good deals or accept bad ones.
- Treat BATNA as ongoing: use realistic (not hypothetical) alternatives, compare like for like, update as information arrives.

**2. "Six Guidelines for 'Getting to Yes'"** (K. Shonk). Full text, ~900 words (excluding comments).
- Handle the people problem directly; take the other side's perspective, listen actively, clarify misunderstandings.
- Look past stated positions to interests; ask "why is this important" and share your own interests so trades across issues appear.
- Let emotions be expressed and named calmly; take breaks when heated.
- Show appreciation: understanding and recognizing merit signals respect without agreeing, which lowers defenses.
- Phrase messages constructively and personally (own your view); blame triggers defensiveness.
- Don't mirror hard stances or attacks ("negotiation jujitsu"): answer with questions, interests, mutual-gain options, objective standards.
- The article's own list is six; options and objective standards appear only in the reader comments (the book covers them).

**3. "Principled Negotiation: Focus on Interests to Create Value"** (K. Shonk). Full text, ~800 words.
- Hard vs. soft is a false choice; the third path is solving the problem on its merits.
- Four elements: separate people from problem, interests over positions, invent options, objective criteria.
- Positions are surface demands; interests are the needs behind them (siblings' party example resolved by costs vs. prep time).
- Brainstorm before committing, suspend judgment, and trade across issues. Options include contingencies, conditions, timing, performance incentives.
- Agree in advance on neutral standards (market value, benchmarks, expert opinion) to cut friction.
- The goal is a deal better than your BATNA, not any deal. Strengthen your alternatives; walking away is disciplined, not failure.

**4. "BATNA and Other Sources of Power at the Negotiation Table"** (PON Staff; Galinsky and Magee research). Full text, ~330 words.
- Three power sources: a strong BATNA, role power (title/position), psychological power (feeling powerful).
- A strong BATNA clarifies options, builds confidence, enables walking away (e.g. buyer finds another equally liked house).
- Role power means you sometimes defer to high-status counterparts.
- Psychological power can be raised just by recalling a time you had power, and improves outcomes.
- Power from any source has similar effects; against a powerful counterpart, raise yours on all three levels.
- A reader comment (not authoritative) adds weakening the other side's BATNA via market knowledge, common in procurement.

**Apply to our buyer agent**
1. Before negotiating, build a normalized comparison (unit price, volume, delivery, payment terms, warranty) for every supplier quote. Never compare headline prices; track the best alternative quote as a live BATNA and refresh it after each reply.
2. Never accept a deal worse than the current best normalized alternative; if all quotes lose to the BATNA, walk away or keep seeking quotes.
3. Ask why before pushing price (deadline, volume, cash flow, inventory). Offer trades across issues (larger volume, faster payment, flexible delivery, longer contract) for a lower total cost.
4. Stay polite and appreciative, never blame; if the supplier turns hostile or pushes hard, don't mirror it. Reply with a question or an interest-based option.
5. Justify asks with objective references (competing quotes, market prices, past orders), and mention real alternatives to raise your leverage. Caution: don't bluff about alternatives that do not exist.

Caveat: these are popularizations of Getting to Yes, not the book. They contain no data on bots or email specifically; mapping to supplier bots is our inference.

5. Justify asks with objective references (competing quotes, market prices, past orders), and mention real alternatives to raise your leverage. Caution: don't bluff about alternatives that do not exist.

Caveat: these are popularizations of Getting to Yes, not the book. They contain no data on bots or email specifically; mapping to supplier bots is our inference.
